rows.question: When does my maternity leave start if my due date is 15 November 2026?
rows.reply:
Under German law, the period before the birth is called the 'Schutzfrist vor der Entbindung', part of Mutterschutz (statutory maternity protection period). Your employer may not employ you "in den letzten sechs Wochen vor der Entbindung", in the last six weeks before delivery, unless you expressly declare that you are willing to work. You can withdraw that declaration at any time, with effect for the future (MuSchG §3(1)).

The six weeks are counted from the expected day of delivery stated in a certificate from a doctor, a midwife or a male midwife ("Entbindungspfleger"). That certificate decides the calculation, not your own estimate (MuSchG §3(1)). So the start of your period is six weeks before the due date on your certificate. If that certificate says 15 November 2026, it is six weeks before that date. The excerpts do not say how the individual days are counted, so they do not give the exact first day.

If the baby is not born on the expected day, the period before the birth becomes shorter or longer to match (MuSchG §3(1)).

After the birth, your employer may not employ you until eight weeks have passed. This extends to twelve weeks:
1. for premature births (Frühgeburten),
2. for multiple births (Mehrlingsgeburten),
3. if a disability of the child is medically established before the eight weeks end. This extension applies only if you apply for it.
If the birth comes early, the period after the birth is also extended by the time the period before the birth was shortened (MuSchG §3(2)).

You should tell your employer that you are pregnant and give the expected day of delivery as soon as you know. If your employer asks, you should provide a certificate from a doctor or midwife that states that day (MuSchG §15). The same kind of certificate also governs maternity pay before the birth under SGB V §24i(3).

For the exact first day of your period, ask your employer, who must apply this rule. For maternity pay, ask your health insurance fund (Krankenkasse).

This is not the same as Elternzeit, the parental leave under the BEEG, which is a separate rule.

rows.question: How long after birth can we apply for Elterngeld without losing money?
rows.reply:
The excerpts do not set an application deadline. What they limit is back payment.

Under BEEG §7(1), Elterngeld (parental allowance) must be applied for in writing ("ist schriftlich zu beantragen"). It is paid retroactively only for the last three Lebensmonate before the start of the Lebensmonat in which the application was received: "rückwirkend nur für die letzten drei Lebensmonate vor Beginn des Lebensmonats geleistet, in dem der Antrag auf Elterngeld eingegangen ist." Months before that window are not paid. The later the application arrives, the more whole months of payment are lost.

BEEG §4(1) says Elterngeld can be drawn from the day of birth ("ab dem Tag der Geburt"). Basiselterngeld can be drawn until the child completes the 14th Lebensmonat. Elterngeld Plus can be drawn until the 32nd Lebensmonat, as long as at least one parent draws it in consecutive Lebensmonate from the 15th onward. BEEG §4(5) extends these periods for a child born at least six, eight, twelve or 16 weeks before the expected date of delivery. The excerpts do not define how a Lebensmonat is counted.

The Elterngeldstelle decides on Elterngeld; the Familienportal refers to "die Entscheidung Ihrer Elterngeldstelle". That office is where to ask about your own application and the months it would cover.

rows.question: How much notice do I have to give my employer for Elternzeit?
rows.reply:
Elternzeit (parental leave (unpaid job-protected leave)) is requested from your employer, not from an authority. The notice period depends on when the leave falls (BEEG §16(1)):

1. For leave up to the child's third birthday: at least seven weeks before the leave begins ("spätestens sieben Wochen").
2. For leave between the third birthday and the child's eighth birthday: at least 13 weeks before the leave begins ("spätestens 13 Wochen").

The request must be made to the employer "in Textform" (in text form). The federal Familienportal explains that this can be, for example, a letter without a signature or an email.

Three further rules in the same section apply to the request:

- If you request leave for the period up to the third birthday, you must at the same time state which periods within two years you will take.
- If there are urgent reasons, a reasonable shorter notice period is possible as an exception ("Bei dringenden Gründen ist ausnahmsweise eine angemessene kürzere Frist möglich").
- If a mother wants leave directly after her maternity protection period after birth, that protection period counts toward the two-year period. If she takes leave directly after holiday that follows the protection period, both count toward the two-year period.

If an employee cannot request leave in time to start directly after the maternity protection period, for a reason she is not responsible for, she can make the request within one week after that reason ends (BEEG §16(2)).

Your employer must certify your Elternzeit to you (BEEG §16(1)).

Giving notice also starts protection against dismissal. From the time leave has been requested, the employer may not dismiss you. This protection begins no earlier than eight weeks before leave up to the third birthday. For leave between the third and eighth birthday, it begins no earlier than 14 weeks before (BEEG §18(1)).

rows.question: How long is maternity protection after the birth if the baby comes early?
rows.reply:
Under Mutterschutz (statutory maternity protection period), an employer may not employ a woman until eight weeks after the birth ("bis zum Ablauf von acht Wochen nach der Entbindung", MuSchG §3(2)). If the baby comes early, two separate rules in MuSchG §3 can lengthen this.

1. Extension to twelve weeks. The period after the birth is extended to twelve weeks in three cases (MuSchG §3(2) sentence 2):
- for premature births ("bei Frühgeburten");
- for multiple births ("bei Mehrlingsgeburten");
- if, before eight weeks after the birth have passed, a doctor diagnoses a disability in the child within the meaning of §2(1) sentence 1 of Book IX of the Social Code. This third extension applies only if the woman applies for it ("nur, wenn die Frau dies beantragt").
This twelve-week extension does not apply to a stillbirth ("Satz 2 gilt nicht bei einer Totgeburt").

2. Adding the days lost before the birth. The six-week period before the birth is counted from the expected date of delivery, and it is shortened if the baby arrives before that date (MuSchG §3(1)). In an early delivery ("Bei vorzeitiger Entbindung"), the period after the birth, whether eight or twelve weeks, is extended by the time the pre-birth period was shortened (MuSchG §3(2) sentence 3).

What this means in the two situations. The statute itself does not define "Frühgeburt". The federal Familienportal explains the difference this way. If the baby is born before the expected date but is not medically a premature birth, the period still totals 14 weeks: it ends not eight weeks after the birth but as many days later as the baby arrived early. If the baby is medically a premature birth (the page gives, as an example, a birth weight under 2,500 grams), protection lasts twelve weeks after the birth.

The Familienportal also says that after the birth you may not work even if you want to. The exception it gives is for school pupils and students, who may resume their studies earlier if they expressly ask. If an employer demands that you work during the protection period, the page says you can turn to your supervisory authority (Aufsichtsbehörde). It names the Krankenkasse as the body to apply to for the disability extension.

rows.question: Can my employer dismiss me while I am pregnant?
rows.reply:
Only in exceptional cases, and only with an authority's prior approval.

The general rule. Under MuSchG §17(1), dismissal of a woman is not permitted ("Die Kündigung gegenüber einer Frau ist unzulässig"):
1. during her pregnancy,
2. until four months after a miscarriage after the twelfth week of pregnancy, and
3. until the end of her protection period after the birth, and at least until four months after the birth.

This Kündigungsschutz (protection against dismissal) applies if your employer knows about the pregnancy, miscarriage or birth when dismissing you, or if you tell them within two weeks of receiving the dismissal ("innerhalb von zwei Wochen nach Zugang der Kündigung"). Missing those two weeks does no harm if the delay was for a reason you are not responsible for and you inform them without delay. The same rules apply to steps your employer takes to prepare a dismissal. The protection applies even if you did not yet know you were pregnant, but you must already have been pregnant when you received the dismissal.

The exception. Under MuSchG §17(2), the highest state authority responsible for occupational safety, or a body it designates, can exceptionally declare a dismissal permissible. This is only possible in special cases that are not connected with your condition during pregnancy, after a miscarriage after the twelfth week, or after the birth. The dismissal must be in writing and must state the reason.

The Familienportal gives these as examples of such special grounds:
- the company is insolvent;
- part of the business is being closed;
- in a small business, the business cannot continue without a qualified replacement;
- you have committed a particularly serious breach of duty.

In these cases your employer must apply in writing to the supervisory authority. Without its consent, the dismissal is invalid ("unwirksam").

If you are dismissed without that consent. The Familienportal says you must bring a claim before the competent labour court, which can establish that the dismissal is legally invalid. It states: "Die Klage müssen Sie normalerweise innerhalb von 3 Wochen erheben, ab Erhalt der schriftlichen Kündigung." That means the claim normally has to be filed within 3 weeks of receiving the written dismissal. If you do not bring a claim, the dismissal is treated as legally effective.

You can file the claim yourself or through a representative, such as a lawyer. If you do not want to file it in writing, you can make it orally at the court office ("mündlich zu Protokoll der Geschäftsstelle beim Arbeitsgericht"). The Familienportal also says you should involve the competent supervisory authority.

If the authority has consented. You can also challenge that consent. Depending on the federal state, this is done by objection or by a court claim. This is a separate procedure. It does not replace the claim before the labour court, and on its own it cannot keep your employment in place.

After the birth. Separate protection against dismissal applies from the point Elternzeit is requested and during Elternzeit (BEEG §18).

The excerpts do not name which body acts as the supervisory authority in Hessen. Whether a particular dismissal is valid is decided by the labour court, and whether a dismissal is declared permissible is decided by the responsible state authority. Those are the places to take your own case.

rows.question: Is there an income limit above which we get no Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes. Under BEEG §1(8), the right to Elterngeld (parental allowance) lapses ("Ein Anspruch entfällt") if the claimant's zu versteuerndes Einkommen (taxable income) in the last completed tax assessment period before the child's birth ("im letzten abgeschlossenen Veranlagungszeitraum vor der Geburt des Kindes") was more than 175,000 euro.

Where another person also meets the conditions, the limit applies to both incomes added together. That other person is someone who also lives in a household with the child, or who meets §1(3) or (4). The claim then lapses if "die Summe des zu versteuernden Einkommens beider Personen mehr als 175 000 Euro beträgt." The federal Familienportal puts it this way: for couples and separated parents the incomes of both parents are added together, and for single parents only their own income counts.

The limit is on zu versteuerndes Einkommen, not gross income. The Familienportal says gross income is usually considerably higher. It says the individual figure is determined by the tax office and appears in the tax assessment notice ("Steuerbescheid"), and that this notice, where available, is to be attached to the application.

If the tax assessment notice for the last completed assessment period is not available when you apply, the law provides two routes (BEEG §8):
- Where the application indicates the limit will probably not be exceeded, Elterngeld is paid subject to revocation if it turns out the limit was exceeded (§8(2)).
- Where it cannot yet be said whether the limit is exceeded, the amount is decided provisionally (§8(3) no. 1).
The Familienportal adds that parents can still apply in that situation.

Earlier births: the Familienportal describes higher limits for earlier births. It gives 200,000 euro for couples and single parents for births from 1 April 2024, and 300,000 euro for couples and 250,000 euro for single parents for births from 1 September 2021 to 31 March 2024. The statutory provision that governs earlier births is not among these excerpts, so this reply does not fix which limit applies to a particular birth date.

Whether the limit affects your family is decided by the Elterngeld office for your district, so that is where to ask about your own case.

rows.question: How many months of Elterngeld can we get in total?
rows.reply:
How many months the law provides depends on which form of Elterngeld (parental allowance) you take, and on some conditions. It does not depend on calendar months: Elterngeld is paid "in Monatsbeträgen für Lebensmonate des Kindes" (monthly amounts for the child's months of life) (BEEG §4(2)). The Familienportal explains that these Lebensmonate begin from the child's date of birth. For example, for a child born on 15 February, the first Lebensmonat runs from 15 February to 14 March.

Basiselterngeld:
- Parents together are entitled to "zwölf Monatsbeträge Basiselterngeld" (twelve monthly amounts) (BEEG §4(3)).
- They get two more months, the Partnermonate, if one parent's employment income is reduced in two Lebensmonate (BEEG §4(3)).
- One parent can have at most twelve monthly amounts of Basiselterngeld (BEEG §4(4)).
- Each parent must draw Elterngeld for at least two Lebensmonate to be entitled at all (BEEG §4(4)).
- Basiselterngeld can be drawn until the child completes the 14th Lebensmonat (BEEG §4(1)).

Elterngeld Plus:
- Instead of one Lebensmonat of Basiselterngeld, a parent can draw two Lebensmonate of Elterngeld Plus (BEEG §4(3)).
- Elterngeld Plus can be drawn until the child completes the 32nd Lebensmonat. From the 15th Lebensmonat onward, this only holds while at least one parent draws it in consecutive Lebensmonate (BEEG §4(1)).

Partnerschaftsbonus:
- On top of the twelve months, one parent can have at most "vier zustehenden Monatsbeträge Partnerschaftsbonus nach § 4b" (four monthly amounts) (BEEG §4(4)).
- The Familienportal describes this as up to 4 additional months of ElterngeldPlus for each parent, if both of you work part-time at the same time.

Months that count as Basiselterngeld:
- Lebensmonate in which a parent receives benefits credited under §3(1) sentence 1 nos. 1 to 3 count as months of Basiselterngeld (BEEG §4(4)).
- The same applies to insurance benefits under §192(5) sentence 2 of the Versicherungsvertragsgesetz (BEEG §4(4)).
- The Familienportal explains that, for the mother, this covers months with Mutterschaftsgeld or other maternity benefits. These months are "verbraucht" (used up) whether or not Basiselterngeld is applied for.

Both parents at the same time:
- Both parents can draw Basiselterngeld at the same time in only one of the child's first twelve Lebensmonate (BEEG §4(6)).
- If one parent draws Elterngeld Plus, that parent can draw it alongside the other parent's Basiselterngeld or Elterngeld Plus (BEEG §4(6)).
- Both can draw Basiselterngeld at the same time for longer in these cases: multiple births, premature births within §4(5), children with a medically established disability, and children who trigger a Geschwisterbonus under §2a (BEEG §4(6)).
- The Familienportal adds that a month of simultaneous Basiselterngeld counts as 2 Basiselterngeld months used.

Premature births (BEEG §4(5)):
- The joint entitlement rises to 13, 14, 15 or 16 monthly amounts of Basiselterngeld. This applies to a child born at least 6, 8, 12 or 16 weeks before the expected date of delivery.
- The per-parent maximum rises in the same way, to 13, 14, 15 or 16 months, plus up to four months of Partnerschaftsbonus.
- Basiselterngeld can then be drawn until the child completes the 15th, 16th, 17th or 18th Lebensmonat.
- Elterngeld Plus still runs until the 32nd Lebensmonat. It must be drawn in consecutive months from the 16th, 17th, 18th or 19th Lebensmonat respectively.
- The expected date is the one shown in the medical certificate or the certificate of a midwife.

Adopted children:
- For adopted children, and children within §1(3) sentence 1 no. 1, Elterngeld can be drawn from when the child is taken in, up to the child's eighth birthday at most (BEEG §4(1)).

In the application you state which Lebensmonate you claim as Basiselterngeld, Elterngeld Plus or Partnerschaftsbonus (BEEG §7(1)).

This sets out the maximums the law provides. How many months your family receives depends on which conditions apply to you. Only the Elterngeldstelle responsible for you decides that, so that is where to ask about your own case.

rows.question: What is the Partnerschaftsbonus and who qualifies?
rows.reply:
The Partnerschaftsbonus (partnership bonus months) is extra Elterngeld Plus for parents who both work part time at the same time. Under BEEG §4b(1), each parent gets an additional monthly amount of Elterngeld Plus for each Lebensmonat in which both conditions are met.

The conditions in BEEG §4b(1) are that both parents:
1. work "nicht weniger als 24 und nicht mehr als 32 Wochenstunden im Durchschnitt des Lebensmonats" (at least 24 and at most 32 hours a week on average over the Lebensmonat), and
2. meet the conditions of BEEG §1. The excerpts available here do not set out what §1 requires.

The official family portal adds that you do not need to work 24 to 32 hours in every single week. What counts is the monthly average.

How it can be taken (BEEG §4b(2) and (3)):
- Each parent can receive at most four monthly amounts of Partnerschaftsbonus.
- It can only be taken for at least two Lebensmonate.
- Both parents must take it at the same time, in consecutive Lebensmonate.

BEEG §4(4) confirms that these up to four bonus amounts come on top of a parent's maximum of twelve monthly amounts of Basiselterngeld. The family portal says the bonus can be used before, between or after the other Elterngeld months, and also if you otherwise receive only Basiselterngeld. It is calculated the same way as Elterngeld Plus.

Single parents. Under BEEG §4c(2), one parent can receive these additional Elterngeld Plus amounts alone. This requires working 24 to 32 hours a week on average in at least two and at most four consecutive Lebensmonate, and one of the grounds in §4c(1) must apply:
1. that parent meets the conditions for the single-parent tax relief under §24b(1) and (3) of the Income Tax Act, and the other parent lives neither with them nor with the child;
2. care by the other parent would endanger the child's welfare within the meaning of §1666(1) and (2) of the Civil Code; or
3. care by the other parent is impossible, in particular because of serious illness or severe disability. Economic reasons and being prevented by other activities do not count.

If one of these grounds arises while both parents are already receiving the bonus, one parent can continue alone under §4c(2) (BEEG §4b(4)). The family portal also says separated parents who raise their child apart can receive the Partnerschaftsbonus.

If the hours turn out differently. Under BEEG §4b(5), the requirement of consecutive months still counts as met if it later turns out that the conditions were not present in every month applied for. The family portal adds the following:
- If you work more or less than planned on average in a Lebensmonat, you must report it to your Elterngeldstelle.
- For any month outside 24 to 32 hours, the bonus for that month must be repaid. If only one parent misses the conditions, both lose the bonus for that month.
- Other months are not affected if the conditions were met in at least two months.

Earlier births. The family portal states that its explanations cover children born after August 2021. Partly different rules apply to children born before 1 September 2021, and the portal refers those parents to their Elterngeldstelle. BEEG §27 also contains a COVID-19 special rule for bonus periods falling wholly or partly before 23 September 2022. For those periods, the income and working-hours figures credibly stated when applying apply if the pandemic made the conditions impossible to meet.

Whether a particular family qualifies is decided by the Elterngeldstelle. That is where to ask about your own case.

rows.question: We forgot to apply for Kindergeld. How far back will they pay?
rows.reply:
Kindergeld (child benefit) is paid retroactively for at most six months. The statute says payment of Kindergeld that has been set is made retroactively "nur für die letzten sechs Monate vor Beginn des Monats, in dem der Antrag auf Kindergeld eingegangen ist": only for the last six months before the start of the month in which the application was received (EStG §70(1)). Earlier months are not paid out. The month your application arrives is what counts, not the month you send it.

The same provision adds that the entitlement itself is not affected by this limit on payment: "Der Anspruch auf Kindergeld nach § 62 bleibt von dieser Auszahlungsbeschränkung unberührt" (EStG §70(1)). The excerpts do not say what follows from this for months beyond the six.

The Familienportal explains that retroactive payment applies where Kindergeld was due but not paid, for example because no application was made. When applying retroactively, you state in the application that you are claiming retroactively and from when you want Kindergeld.

Kindergeld must be applied for in writing (BKGG §9(1)). The Familienportal adds that an electronic application is also possible, and that it is made at the Familienkasse of your Agentur für Arbeit. The Familienkasse sets Kindergeld by formal decision and pays it (EStG §70(1)). It decides which months you are paid for, so it is the place to ask about your own case. The Bundesagentur für Arbeit's free service line for questions about applying is 0800 4 555530.

rows.question: How quickly do we have to register the birth at the Standesamt?
rows.reply:
The law requires the birth to be reported to the Standesamt (civil registry office) responsible for the place where the child was born "binnen einer Woche" (within one week) (PStG §18(1)). The report can come from either of two sources:

1. From the persons named in PStG §19, orally or in writing. These persons must substantiate the birth ("glaubhaft zu machen").
2. From the institutions named in PStG §20, in writing.

If a child is stillborn, the report must be made at the latest on the third working day after the birth (PStG §18(1)).

The Familienportal explains how this works in practice. If your child is born in a hospital, birth centre or maternity clinic, the facility notifies the responsible Standesamt and sends the birth certificate issued at the birth. If your child is born at home, the midwife or doctor issues that certificate, and you must present it to the responsible Standesamt within one week.

One Familienportal checklist describes the period as "7 Werktagen" (7 working days). The statute says "binnen einer Woche", and the statute's wording is what governs.

The Familienportal also says the Standesamt in the place of birth publishes on its website which other documents it needs from you. The Standesamt where your child is born is the office to ask about your own registration.

rows.question: What do we need to bring to the Standesamt to register the birth?
rows.reply:
Under PStV §33, when a birth is registered the Standesamt (civil registry office) is to ask for these documents:

1. If the parents are married to each other: your marriage certificate or a certified extract from the marriage register. Also bring your own birth certificates if the details of your births do not appear on the marriage certificate.
2. If the parents are not married to each other: the mother's birth certificate. If paternity has already been acknowledged, also bring the acknowledgement declarations, the father's birth certificate and, where they exist, the declarations of joint parental custody.
3. The parents' identity card, passport or another recognised passport substitute.
4. If the birth is reported in person: a certificate of the birth issued by a doctor or midwife who was present at the birth.

The marriage certificate is required even if the marriage has ended. The Standesamt may also ask for further documents where it needs them to prove the details given (PStV §33).

If neither parent is German, PStV §34(1) says the Standesamt will ask at registration whether a parent holds an unlimited right of residence ("unbefristetes Aufenthaltsrecht"), or a residence permit as a Swiss national or a Swiss national's family member under the 1999 EU–Switzerland free movement agreement. The Standesamt uses this to check whether the child acquired German citizenship at birth under StAG §4(3). StAG §4(3) attaches two conditions to one parent: five years of lawful habitual residence in Germany, and one of those residence rights. The Standesamt then obtains written information from the Ausländerbehörde and makes that check itself (PStV §34(2) and (3)).

The Familienportal guidance adds the following. If the child was born in a hospital, birth centre or maternity clinic, the facility notifies the Standesamt and sends it the birth certificate from the birth. If the child was born at home, the midwife or doctor issues that certificate, and you must present it to the Standesamt within one week. The same page says you must register the child within one week at the Standesamt responsible for the place of birth. The Familienportal checklist puts this as "innerhalb von 7 Werktagen" (within 7 working days).

Which further documents you need is listed on the website of the Standesamt in the town where your child is born, the Familienportal says. That Standesamt is where to ask about your own registration.

rows.question: Does my Krankenkasse pay for a midwife?
rows.reply:
Yes, the statutory health insurance law gives an insured woman an entitlement to midwife help. Under SGB V §24d, "Die Versicherte hat während der Schwangerschaft, bei und nach der Entbindung Anspruch auf ärztliche Betreuung sowie auf Hebammenhilfe". So an insured woman is entitled to help from a Hebamme (midwife) during pregnancy, at the birth and after it. This includes the examinations to establish the pregnancy and prenatal check-ups ("Untersuchungen zur Feststellung der Schwangerschaft und zur Schwangerenvorsorge").

The same section sets two further rules:

- Midwife help for postnatal care ("Wochenbettbetreuung") is available until twelve weeks after the birth ("bis zum Ablauf von zwölf Wochen nach der Geburt"). Further services need a doctor's order ("bedürfen der ärztlichen Anordnung").
- If the mother cannot care for the child after the birth, the insured child is itself entitled to the midwife services that relate to the child.

The Familienportal puts it the same way. Every woman with statutory health insurance is entitled to support from a Hebamme. If you are privately insured, the portal says you should check with your insurer beforehand which services it covers.

Whether your own care is covered is a matter for your Krankenkasse (statutory health insurer), so ask them about your own case.

rows.question: When are the first check-ups for the baby?
rows.reply:
The Kinder-Richtlinie (the federal directive on early detection of illness in children) sets out ten check-ups in the first six years of life. Each can only be used within its set period, allowing for a tolerance window ("Toleranzgrenze") (Kinder-RL §2).

The first check-ups:
- U1: immediately after birth ("Unmittelbar nach der Geburt"). It has no tolerance window. It should take place within the first 30 minutes after the birth ("innerhalb der ersten 30 Minuten nach der Geburt"). If no doctor is present at the birth but a midwife is, the midwife should carry it out (Kinder-RL §3(1)).
- U2: 3rd to 10th day of life ("3.-10. Lebenstag"). Tolerance window: 3rd to 14th day of life.
- U3: 4th to 5th week of life ("4.-5. Lebenswoche"). Tolerance window: 3rd to 8th week of life.
- U4: 3rd to 4th month of life. Tolerance window: 2nd to 4½th month.
- U5: 6th to 7th month of life. Tolerance window: 5th to 8th month.
- U6: 10th to 12th month of life. Tolerance window: 9th to 14th month.

The later check-ups are:
- U7: 21st to 24th month. Tolerance window: 20th to 27th month.
- U7a: 34th to 36th month. Tolerance window: 33rd to 38th month.
- U8: 46th to 48th month. Tolerance window: 43rd to 50th month.
- U9: 60th to 64th month. Tolerance window: 58th to 66th month.

All of these are in Kinder-RL §2.

For babies born prematurely, the same periods must still be kept ("Auch bei Frühgeborenen sind die Untersuchungszeiträume einzuhalten"). The premature birth is taken into account when the results are assessed (Kinder-RL §2).

Children are entitled to these early-detection examinations until they turn 18 (Kinder-RL §1(1)). They may only be carried out by doctors who have the knowledge, experience, professional authorisation and facilities to provide them, unless the directive provides otherwise (Kinder-RL §1(5)).

The figures above come from the version of the directive in force from 1 January 2026. The Gemeinsamer Bundesausschuss page notes that the version it currently offers does not yet include a decision that came into force on 20 August 2026. For the current text, check the G-BA's Kinder-Richtlinie page.

rows.question: What is Mutterschaftsgeld and when do I apply for it?
rows.reply:
What it is

Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity pay from the health insurer) is paid "für die Zeit der Schutzfristen vor und nach der Entbindung sowie für den Entbindungstag": for the maternity protection periods before and after the birth, and for the day of the birth itself (MuSchG §19, SGB V §24i(3)). The federal family portal says these periods "beginnen normalerweise 6 Wochen vor dem errechneten Geburtstermin und enden 8 Wochen nach der Geburt": they normally begin 6 weeks before the calculated due date and end 8 weeks after the birth.

Who pays it depends on how you are insured:

- If you are a member of a statutory health insurer (gesetzliche Krankenkasse), you receive it under the Fifth Book of the Social Code (SGB V) (MuSchG §19(1)). The family portal describes it as "das Mutterschaftsgeld Ihrer Krankenkasse". Under SGB V §24i(1), it goes to members who are entitled to sickness benefit when unable to work, or who are not paid wages because of the protection periods. It also goes to women whose employment ends immediately before the protection period begins, if they were a member of a health insurer on the last day of employment.
- If you are not a member of a statutory health insurer, you receive it at the expense of the federal government, "insgesamt höchstens 210 Euro" (at most 210 euros in total). It is paid "auf Antrag vom Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung": on application, by the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung (MuSchG §19(2)).

How much (statutory members)

For members who are in employment when the protection period before the birth begins, it is the average net daily pay from the last three calendar months settled before that period. It is capped at "höchstens 13 Euro für den Kalendertag" (at most 13 euros per calendar day) (SGB V §24i(2)). Women whose employment ended immediately before the protection period, and other members, receive it at the level of sickness benefit (Krankengeld) (SGB V §24i(2)).

If average daily pay is above 13 euros, the employer pays the difference as a supplement, the Zuschuss zum Mutterschaftsgeld (MuSchG §20(1); SGB V §24i(2)). If a woman works for several employers, they pay it in shares (MuSchG §20(2)). Where employment ended by a permitted dismissal under §17(2), or the employer cannot pay because of insolvency, the body responsible for paying Mutterschaftsgeld pays the supplement instead (MuSchG §20(3)).

The claim "ruht" (is suspended) for as long as, and to the extent that, you receive wages, earned income or holiday compensation subject to contributions. One-off payments are excepted (SGB V §24i(4)).

When to apply

The excerpts do not set an application deadline or a timing for applying. They do state what payment depends on. For payment before the birth, the decisive document is "das Zeugnis eines Arztes oder einer Hebamme" stating the expected day of delivery. This is a certificate from a doctor or a midwife (SGB V §24i(3)). For statutory members, ask your Krankenkasse about how and when to apply. If you are not statutorily insured, the application goes to the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung (MuSchG §19(2)).

Link to Elterngeld

Mutterschaftsgeld under SGB V and the employer supplement under MuSchG §20 are offset against Elterngeld for the period from the day of the birth. Mutterschaftsgeld under MuSchG §19(2), the payment for women who are not statutory members, is not offset (BEEG §3(1)). The family portal puts it this way: if the maternity benefits for the same child are higher than Elterngeld, you receive only the maternity benefits. If Elterngeld is higher, you receive the difference as Elterngeld on top.

rows.question: We are not married. Is my partner automatically the legal father?
rows.reply:
No. Under BGB §1592, a man is the legal father of a child in one of three cases only: 1. he is married to the child's mother at the time of the birth ("zum Zeitpunkt der Geburt mit der Mutter des Kindes verheiratet"); 2. he has acknowledged paternity ("die Vaterschaft anerkannt hat"); or 3. his paternity has been determined by a court under BGB §1600d or §182(1) of the Act on Proceedings in Family Matters. Where the parents are not married at the birth, the federal family portal states that the father must make a Vaterschaftsanerkennung (acknowledgement of paternity) to count as the legal father. It is voluntary and requires the mother's consent.

Rules that apply to the acknowledgement (BGB §1594):
- It may be made before the child is born (§1594(4)).
- It is not effective while another man's paternity exists (§1594(2)). For example, under §1592 no. 1, a man married to the mother at the birth is the father.
- An acknowledgement made subject to a condition or a time limit is invalid (§1594(3)).
- Its legal effects can only be relied on from the time it becomes effective, unless the law provides otherwise (§1594(1)).

rows.question: How do unmarried parents get joint custody?
rows.reply:
Under BGB §1626a(1), parents who are not married to each other when the child is born have joint parental custody in three cases:

1. They declare that they want to take on custody jointly. These are Sorgeerklärungen (declarations of joint custody).
2. They marry each other.
3. The Familiengericht transfers custody to them jointly.

In all other cases, the mother has custody (§1626a(3)).

The first step is recognised fatherhood. The Familienportal says the other parent must first be legally recognised as the father. That happens when he acknowledges the child as his own with the mother's consent, or when a court establishes paternity. Acknowledging paternity does not by itself give custody. A Sorgeerklärung or a court decision is still needed.

For the declaration route, the Familienportal says Sorgeerklärungen are made "zum Beispiel beim Jugendamt oder bei einem Notar" (for example at the Jugendamt or with a notary). They can also be made before the birth.

For the court route, one parent applies to the Familiengericht (§1626a(2)). The court transfers custody, or part of it, to both parents jointly "wenn die Übertragung dem Kindeswohl nicht widerspricht" (if the transfer does not contradict the child's welfare). If the other parent puts forward no reasons against joint custody, and none are otherwise apparent, the law presumes that joint custody does not contradict the child's welfare. The Familienportal adds two points. Such reasons must be raised within a period the Familiengericht sets. In that situation, the court decides in a simplified procedure, without hearing the Jugendamt and without hearing the parents in person.

For the marriage route, marrying after the birth also establishes joint custody.

An entry is made in the Sorgeregister (custody register) kept at the responsible Jugendamt in two of these cases (SGB VIII §58(1)):
- when Sorgeerklärungen under §1626a(1) No. 1 are made;
- when custody has been transferred to the parents jointly, in whole or in part, by a final court decision.

Unmarried parents are entitled to advice on making a Sorgeerklärung and on the possibility of a court transfer of joint custody (SGB VIII §18(2)). Your responsible Jugendamt advises on all questions of parental custody.

rows.question: Will our baby automatically be German if we are both Indian citizens?
rows.reply:
Not by birth in Germany alone. The law sets out specific routes, each with conditions.

Through a parent: a child acquires deutsche Staatsangehörigkeit (citizenship) by birth if a parent holds German Staatsangehörigkeit (StAG §4(1)).

Through birth in Germany to foreign parents: a child born in Germany ("Geburt im Inland") to foreign parents acquires German Staatsangehörigkeit if one parent meets both of these conditions (StAG §4(3)):
1. has lawfully had their habitual residence in Germany for five years ("seit fünf Jahren rechtmäßig seinen gewöhnlichen Aufenthalt im Inland"), and
2. holds an unlimited right of residence ("unbefristetes Aufenthaltsrecht"), or, as a Swiss national or a Swiss national's family member, a residence permit under the 1999 EU–Switzerland free movement agreement.
The acquisition is entered in the birth register ("Geburtenregister") where the birth is recorded (StAG §4(3)).

How it is checked: when the birth is registered, the Standesamt asks whether a parent holds an unlimited right of residence (PStV §34(1)). If the information indicates the conditions are met, it obtains written confirmation from the Ausländerbehörde on whether the information is correct and whether the parent had five years' lawful habitual residence at the time of the birth. It also does this if the parents give no information or the Standesamt doubts it, and then asks about both parents (PStV §34(2)). The Standesamt examines whether the child acquired German Staatsangehörigkeit by birth and records the result (PStV §34(3)).

Whether your child meets these conditions is not something this service can say. The Standesamt that registers the birth makes that check, so that is where to ask about your own child.

Separately, residence rules for a child born in Germany are in AufenthG §33. A residence permit is granted to the child of the authorities' own motion ("von Amts wegen") if at the time of birth both parents, or the parent with sole custody, hold an Aufenthaltserlaubnis, a Niederlassungserlaubnis or an Erlaubnis zum Daueraufenthalt – EU. If only one parent holds one of these, a permit may be granted. If a parent holds a visa or may stay visa-free at the time of birth, the child's stay counts as permitted until that visa or visa-free stay ends.

The excerpts do not cover whether your child acquires Indian citizenship. For that, contact the Indian embassy or consulate responsible for your area.

rows.question: Does our newborn need a residence permit?
rows.reply:
The law sets out several situations for a child born in Germany to foreign parents, depending on the parents' own status at the time of birth. Which one applies to your child is decided by the responsible authority, not here.

When a child born in Germany is given an Aufenthaltserlaubnis (residence permit) (AufenthG §33):
- If at least one parent holds an Aufenthaltserlaubnis, a "Niederlassungserlaubnis" or an "Erlaubnis zum Daueraufenthalt – EU", the child "kann … von Amts wegen eine Aufenthaltserlaubnis erteilt werden": the permit may be granted on the authority's own initiative, notwithstanding §§5 and 29(1) no. 2 of the AufenthG.
- If at the time of birth both parents, or the parent who alone has custody ("der allein personensorgeberechtigte Elternteil"), hold one of those three permits, the child's Aufenthaltserlaubnis "wird … von Amts wegen erteilt": it is granted on the authority's own initiative.
- If the mother or father holds a visa at the time of birth, or may stay without a visa, the child's stay "gilt bis zum Ablauf des Visums oder des rechtmäßigen visumfreien Aufenthalts als erlaubt": it counts as permitted until that visa or lawful visa-free stay ends.

A related rule on German citizenship by birth (StAG §4):
- A child acquires German citizenship by birth if a parent is a German citizen (§4(1)).
- A child of foreign parents born in Germany acquires German citizenship if one parent (1) has had lawful habitual residence in Germany for five years and (2) has an unlimited right of residence ("ein unbefristetes Aufenthaltsrecht"), or holds a residence permit as a Swiss national or a Swiss national's family member under the EU–Switzerland free movement agreement of 21 June 1999 (§4(3)). The acquisition is entered in the birth register.
The excerpts do not say what a child who acquires German citizenship needs in terms of residence status.

How this is checked at birth registration (PStV §34): when the birth is reported, the Standesamt asks whether a parent has an unlimited right of residence or the Swiss-agreement permit. Where the stated details meet those conditions, where the parents give no details, or where the Standesamt doubts them, it obtains written information from the Ausländerbehörde. That information covers whether the details are correct and whether the parent had lawful habitual residence in Germany for five years at the time of birth. The Standesamt then examines whether the child acquired German citizenship by birth and records the result.

Whether your child needs a residence permit, receives one automatically, or acquired German citizenship depends on your own permits and residence history. Only the responsible authority decides that. The excerpts do not name which body grants the child's permit. For your own case, approach your local Ausländerbehörde. rows.question: We are getting Mutterschaftsgeld. Does that reduce our Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
The law says Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity pay from the health insurer) is counted against Elterngeld (parental allowance). How this affects your own payments is decided by the Elterngeld office for your district, so that is where to ask about your case.

What the law says:

- BEEG §3(1) lists the income that is "auf das … Elterngeld … angerechnet" (offset against Elterngeld). The first item is Mutterschaftsleistungen (maternity benefits) for the time from the day of the child's birth. That covers two things:
  - Mutterschaftsgeld under the Fifth Book of the Social Code, which MuSchG §19(1) says a member of a statutory health insurer receives for the protection periods before and after the birth.
  - The employer's supplement to Mutterschaftsgeld under MuSchG §20.
- One exception: the Mutterschaftsgeld under MuSchG §19(2) is not offset. That is the payment of at most 210 euros from the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung for women who are not members of a statutory health insurer.
- The 300 euros of Elterngeld that BEEG §3(2) otherwise protects from offsetting does not apply here. The protection holds "soweit nicht Einnahmen nach Absatz 1 Satz 1 Nummer 1 bis 3 auf das Elterngeld anzurechnen sind", and maternity benefits are item 1.
- If the benefits are due for only part of a Lebensmonat of the child, they are offset only against the matching part of the Elterngeld (BEEG §3(1)).

What the official Familienportal adds, for maternity benefits received for the same child:

- They are offset in full, and day by day.
- If the maternity benefits are higher than the Elterngeld, only the maternity benefits are paid.
- If the Elterngeld is higher, the difference is paid as Elterngeld on top of the maternity benefits.
- Months in which maternity benefits for that child are due "gelten bei Ihnen als Monate mit Basiselterngeld" (count for you as months of Basiselterngeld). A single day of entitlement in a month is enough for this.
- The benefits are offset only against the mother's Elterngeld, not against the father's.

rows.question: Can I work while receiving Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes. Working part-time does not by itself rule out Elterngeld (parental allowance), but the law sets a limit on hours, and earnings reduce the payment.

The hours limit. One condition for Elterngeld is that you are not working, or not working full time: "keine oder keine volle Erwerbstätigkeit ausübt" (BEEG §1(1) no. 4). The law says a person is not working full time if any one of these applies (BEEG §1(6)):
1. their working time does not exceed 32 hours a week, averaged over the month of the child's life ("32 Wochenstunden im Durchschnitt des Lebensmonats");
2. they are in employment for vocational training; or
3. they work as a suitable childminder within the meaning of §§23 and 43 of Book VIII of the Social Code.
The law also counts as working anyone who is temporarily not working while they are in an employment relationship or self-employed (BEEG §1(6a)).

How earnings affect the amount. For months after the birth in which you earn less than you did before the birth, Elterngeld is paid as a percentage of the difference between the two incomes. For this calculation, pre-birth income is counted up to at most 2,770 euros (BEEG §2(3)). The official Familienportal page notes that working part-time can make Elterngeld Plus worthwhile. The statute says that instead of one month of Basiselterngeld, you can receive two months of Elterngeld Plus (BEEG §4(3)).

What you must report. If your application states that you expect to have earnings while receiving Elterngeld, the amount is decided provisionally (BEEG §8(3) no. 3). After the payment period ends, you must prove your actual earnings for that time (BEEG §8(1)). If your application states that you expect no earnings, Elterngeld is paid subject to revocation in case you do have earnings (BEEG §8(2)). For employees, the Familienportal lists a certificate from your employer of your working hours during the Elterngeld period. For self-employed people, it lists your own statement of your previous working hours and your working hours during the period.

The Familienportal explanations apply to children born after August 2021. It says partly different rules apply to children born before 1 September 2021, and it directs those parents to their Elterngeldstelle.

This explains the general rule only. Your Elterngeldstelle decides your application and the amount, so that is where to ask about your own hours and earnings.

rows.question: Where and how do we apply for Kindergeld?
rows.reply:
Where to apply: the application goes to the Familienkasse. Under BKGG §13(1), the Familienkasse responsible for receiving the application and deciding on the claim is the one for the district where the entitled person has their residence (Wohnsitz). If there is no residence in Germany, it is the one for the district of their habitual residence. If there is neither, it is the one for the district where they work. In all other cases it is the Familienkasse Bayern Nord. The Familienportal says to apply at the Familienkasse of your Agentur für Arbeit, which is usually responsible for processing a Kindergeld (child benefit) application.

How to apply: Kindergeld must be applied for in writing. BKGG §9(1) says it is "schriftlich zu beantragen". Besides the entitled person, anyone with a legitimate interest in the payment may also apply. According to the Familienportal, the application can be electronic or written, using the Familienkassen form. You can fill it in online, then print and sign it. For newborn children, you can submit it fully online with a valid ELSTER certificate, with no printing or handwritten signature. The application must state your tax identification number and your child's.

Supporting documents: according to the Bundesagentur für Arbeit, for a child under 18 you normally only need to give your own tax identification number and your child's. For a child over 18, additional proof is needed, for example an internship confirmation or a school certificate. If the child was born abroad or lives abroad, include a copy of the foreign birth certificate, or another official document that certifies the birth. Documents can be sent online to the responsible Familienkasse. If more documents are needed, the Familienkasse will tell you, and give you a date to provide them by. If they are not provided in time, the application may be delayed or refused.

Which parent applies: Kindergeld is paid to only one person per child (BKGG §3(1)). If the child lives in the parents' shared household, the parents decide between themselves who is the entitled person. If they do not decide, the family court decides on application (BKGG §3(2)).

Late applications: the Familienportal says Kindergeld can be paid retroactively for up to 6 months, where it was due but not paid, for example because no application was made. To do this, state in the application that you are applying retroactively and from when you want Kindergeld.

Questions about applying: the Bundesagentur für Arbeit has a free service number, 0800 4 555530. The Familienkasse decides on the claim, so it is the place to take questions about your own application.

rows.question: What are the Elterngeld rules for a self-employed parent in Bavaria?
rows.reply:
Bavaria is outside the states this product covers. It covers federal law, Hessen state procedures and the Indian consular track, so Bavarian application procedures are not described here. For those, go to the Elterngeldstelle responsible for your district in Bavaria. That office decides Elterngeld (parental allowance) applications there, so it is where to ask about your own case.

The rules below are federal law (BEEG) and are not specific to any state.

Who can claim. Under BEEG §1(1), a person can claim if they meet all four conditions:
1. they live or ordinarily stay in Germany
2. they live in one household with the child
3. they care for and bring up the child themselves
4. they do no work, or do not work full time

Under §1(6), a person is not working full time if any of these applies:
1. their working time does not exceed 32 hours a week on average over the Lebensmonat
2. they are in employment for vocational training
3. they work as a qualified Kindertagespflegeperson

Under §1(6a), self-employed people who are temporarily not working still count as working: "selbständig erwerbstätig sind".

Income limit. Under §1(8), there is no claim if taxable income in the last completed Veranlagungszeitraum before the birth was more than 175,000 euros. Where another person also meets the conditions in §1(1) No. 2, (3) or (4), the combined taxable income of both counts.

How the amount is set. Under §2(1), Elterngeld is 67 percent of income from work before the birth. It is paid up to a maximum of 1,800 euros a month for full Lebensmonate in which the person has no income from work. Income from work explicitly includes positive income from "Land- und Forstwirtschaft, Gewerbebetrieb und selbständiger Arbeit" that is taxable in Germany. It is calculated under §§2c to 2f, as the monthly average in the Bemessungszeitraum under §2b.

The excerpts include §2c, but that section covers employment income only. They do not include §2b or the provisions on how self-employed income is determined, so this reply cannot say which period or which documents are used for self-employed income.

Under §2(2), the 67 percent rises towards 100 percent where pre-birth income was below 1,000 euros. It falls towards 65 percent where pre-birth income was above 1,200 euros. Under §2(3), if you earn less after the birth than before, Elterngeld is paid as that percentage of the difference. Pre-birth income counts up to at most 2,770 euros for this purpose. Under §2(4), the minimum is 300 euros.

Provisional decisions. These matter often for self-employed people. Under §8(3), the amount is decided provisionally, on the information made credible, until proof is provided, if any of these applies:
1. at the time of application, the tax assessment (Steuerbescheid) for the last completed Veranlagungszeitraum before the birth is not available, and it cannot yet be said whether the §1(8) amounts are exceeded
2. income from work before the birth cannot be determined
3. according to the application, the person is expected to have income from work during the Bezugszeitraum

Under §8(1), where expected income was stated in the application, actual income for that period must be proven after the Bezugszeitraum ends.

Under §8(2), Elterngeld is paid subject to revocation in two cases:
- the application says no income from work is expected, but there is income
- the tax assessment is missing, and the stated income later turns out to exceed the §1(8) amounts

Duration. Under §4(1), Elterngeld is paid as Basiselterngeld or Elterngeld Plus, from the day of birth. Basiselterngeld can be drawn until the child completes the 14th Lebensmonat. Elterngeld Plus can be drawn until the 32nd Lebensmonat, as long as at least one parent draws it in consecutive Lebensmonate from the 15th.

Only the Elterngeldstelle decides whether and how much Elterngeld a particular parent receives.

rows.question: Based on our situation, will our Elterngeld application be approved?
rows.reply:
Whether your Elterngeld (parental allowance) application will be approved is a decision about your family's individual case. This service cannot assess it or predict the outcome. Only your Elterngeldstelle decides it, and the excerpts show this: a decision of 'Ihrer Elterngeldstelle' can only be reviewed if you lodge an objection ('Widerspruch') against the Elterngeld notice. Because your Elterngeldstelle makes the decision, it is the place to ask about your own case.

These are the general conditions the law sets out.

Who is entitled (BEEG §1(1)). A person is entitled who:
1. has a residence or habitual abode in Germany,
2. lives in one household with their child,
3. cares for and brings up this child themselves, and
4. is not working, or not working full-time.

Under §1(6), a person is not working full-time if their working time does not exceed 32 hours a week on average over the Lebensmonat. It also covers a person in vocational training employment or working as a qualified childminder.

Parents without EU free-movement rights (BEEG §1(7)). Such a parent is entitled only if they hold certain residence titles. These include:
- a settlement permit ('Niederlassungserlaubnis') or EU long-term residence permit,
- an EU Blue Card, ICT card or Mobile ICT card,
- a residence permit that entitles or entitled them to work for at least six months.

The statute excludes residence permits granted for certain purposes. These include training, study, au-pair or seasonal work, and job-seeking. Some humanitarian permits are excluded too, though §1(7) nos. 3 to 5 restore entitlement for them in further cases.

Income limit (BEEG §1(8)). The entitlement lapses if the person's 'zu versteuerndes Einkommen' in the last completed assessment period before the birth was more than 175 000 euro. If another person also meets the conditions, the limit applies to the sum of both persons' income.

The application (BEEG §7(1)). Elterngeld must be applied for in writing ('schriftlich zu beantragen'). It is paid retroactively only for the last three Lebensmonate before the start of the Lebensmonat in which the application is received. Earlier months are not paid.

If you disagree with a decision, the excerpts state that an objection can only be lodged in writing with your Elterngeldstelle within one month of receiving the notice.

rows.question: How much tax will we save if I switch to Steuerklasse 3 before the birth?
rows.reply:
How much tax you would save by switching Steuerklasse is a tax calculation for your household, and this product does not calculate tax owed or saved, or advise on which Steuerklasse to choose. A Steuerberater or your Finanzamt is where to take that question.

What the excerpts do cover is how a Steuerklasse change before the birth feeds into Elterngeld:

- A change of Steuerklasse before the birth "kann sich ... auf die Höhe Ihrer Steuern und Ihrer Sozialabgaben auswirken" (can affect your taxes and social contributions).
- For the simplified calculation of the "Elterngeld-Netto", the newest Steuerklasse counts. The older one is used only if it applied for longer within the whole Bemessungszeitraum (assessment period) than the newer one. The same applies to other deduction data, such as the number of child allowances.
- Changing Steuerklasse again after the birth no longer affects Elterngeld.
- In the statute, the income tax deduction is based on the Steuerklasse and any factor under § 39f of the Income Tax Act. Steuerklasse VI is disregarded (BEEG §2e(3)).
- For income from employment, the Bemessungszeitraum is "die zwölf Kalendermonate vor dem Kalendermonat der Geburt" (the twelve calendar months before the month of birth) (BEEG §2b(1)). Some months are left out unless you apply for them to count: months with Elterngeld for an older child, months under the Mutterschutz protection periods or with Mutterschaftsgeld, months of illness mainly caused by the pregnancy, and months of military or civilian service.
- The Elterngeldstelle calculates the Elterngeld-Netto itself, using a simplified method, so the result can differ from the net pay on your payslip.

The Elterngeldstelle decides your Elterngeld, so that is where to ask about the effect on your own claim.
